metadata.title: Predicting cross-national sex differences in large-scale assessments of students' reading literacy, mathematics, and science achievement: Evidence from PIRLS and TIMSS

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS and TIMSS achievement scores that are already scaled and standardized by IEA procedures, including the use of five plausible values per surveyed year for the cognitive achievement outcomes. The paper does not report applying student/sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight methods in the macro-level regression analyses of country-level sex differences. Because the dependent variables are country-level standardized sex differences (Cohen’s d) derived from IEA-scaled plausible values, the manuscript focuses on regression at the country level rather than re-estimating achievement models from microdata. The analytic sample is restricted to countries that participated in each assessment year for the main analyses, and the authors also run robustness checks including all countries regardless of the number of cohorts.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe any missing-data handling strategy for the macro-level regression dataset (e.g., how missing country-year macro indicators or incomplete country participation were handled). This is a reporting gap because the analysis relies on year- and country-specific macro predictors and on plausible-value-based sex differences; without documentation, it is unclear whether missingness was addressed via exclusion, imputation, or availability-based filtering. Given that the authors report using only countries participating in each year for the main analyses, missingness may have been handled implicitly through listwise availability, but the manuscript does not state this explicitly.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Main analyses include only those countries that participated in each assessment year used for the respective PIRLS/TIMSS waves (countries-by-year inclusion is shown in Table 1). The study uses four PIRLS cohorts (2001, 2006, 2011, 2016) for grade 4 reading literacy and five TIMSS cohorts for grade 4 (2003–2019) and grade 8 (1995–2019), with sex differences computed from IEA-scaled plausible values. For the regression analyses, the dependent variables are country-level Cohen’s d sex differences averaged across plausible values using Rubin (1987) rules; robustness analyses rerun regressions including all countries regardless of the number of cohorts. Additional robustness analyses restrict to countries mandating schooling up to at least grade 8 and re-analyze bottom/top 25% performance subsets selected by the first plausible value.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2001-2016 Grade 4 Reading literacy (overall score; plausible values averaged)
main_findings.target_variable: Reading literacy sex difference (Cohen's d, girls vs boys)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Single-country regression weights on Cohen's d (plausible-value-specific regressions combined via Rubin rules): GDP per capita β = −0.21; Gini Index β = −0.19; GGI β = 0.23; GPI β = 0.27; GET β = 0.08; GEP/GES β = −0.07. Effect-size interpretation uses Cohen’s d thresholds (0.2/0.5/0.8) and Pearson’s r thresholds for standardized regression coefficients.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2001-2016 Grade 4 reading literacy the study leveraged GDP per capita, Gini Index, Gender Gap Index, Gender Parity Index, and government education expenditure to predict the country-level sex difference in reading literacy (Cohen’s d), finding that girls’ reading advantages were smaller in more prosperous and less economically equal countries (β = −0.21 and β = −0.19) but larger in more gender-equal countries (GGI β = 0.23; GPI β = 0.27). This indicates that national gender equality—especially in access to education and broader gender gaps—may be more relevant than overall education spending for sustaining girls’ reading advantages, though the analysis is correlational and based on country-level macro predictors rather than causal identification.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 4 Mathematics (overall score; plausible values averaged)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics sex difference (Cohen's d, girls vs boys)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Single regression weights on Cohen's d: GDP per capita β = −0.39; GEP β = −0.39; GET β = −0.32; GGI β = −0.39; Gini Index β = 0.16; GPI β = 0.04 (not meaningful).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 4 mathematics the study leveraged GDP per capita, education spending (GEP and GET), Gender Gap Index, and Gini Index to predict the country-level sex difference in mathematics (Cohen’s d), finding that boys’ mathematics advantages were larger in more prosperous, more gender-equal, and more educationally invested countries (GDP β = −0.39; GEP β = −0.39; GET β = −0.32; GGI β = −0.39). This indicates that early mathematics gender gaps may widen where gender equality and education investment are higher, suggesting that policy should pair investment with targeted support to ensure equitable participation and interest development for both sexes, while noting that the study does not establish causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 1995-2019 Grade 8 Mathematics (overall score; plausible values averaged)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics sex difference (Cohen's d, girls vs boys)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Single regression weights on Cohen's d: GET β = −0.25; GES β = −0.12; GDP per capita β = 0.12; GPI β = 0.14; GGI β = −0.12; Gini Index β = −0.03 (not meaningful).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 1995-2019 Grade 8 mathematics the study leveraged government education expenditure, GDP per capita, Gender Parity Index, Gender Gap Index, and Gini Index to predict the country-level sex difference in mathematics (Cohen’s d), finding that larger education investment was associated with larger boys’ advantages (GET β = −0.25; GES β = −0.12) while prosperity and enrollment parity showed smaller effects that reduced boys’ relative advantage (GDP β = 0.12; GPI β = 0.14). This indicates that at older ages, mathematics sex gaps may be less consistently tied to prosperity and more sensitive to how education systems allocate resources, implying that policy should monitor whether investment translates into equitable learning opportunities rather than reinforcing gendered subject trajectories.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 4 Science (overall score; plausible values averaged)
main_findings.target_variable: Science sex difference (Cohen's d, girls vs boys)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Single regression weights on Cohen's d: GDP per capita β = −0.36; GEP β = −0.31; Gini Index β = 0.20; GGI β = −0.23; GPI and GEP/GPI effects not meaningful (GEP and GPI β range −0.07 to −0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 4 science the study leveraged GDP per capita, primary education spending (GEP), Gini Index, and Gender Gap Index to predict the country-level sex difference in science (Cohen’s d), finding that boys’ science advantages were larger in more prosperous and more educationally invested countries (GDP β = −0.36; GEP β = −0.31) and in more gender-equal contexts (GGI β = −0.23), with an additional small positive association for economic equality (Gini β = 0.20). This indicates that early science gender gaps may be shaped by national prosperity and gender equality in ways that interact with how education systems fund and structure learning, suggesting that equity-oriented science initiatives should be designed alongside investment rather than assumed to be automatically gender-neutral.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 1995-2019 Grade 8 Science (overall score; plausible values averaged)
main_findings.target_variable: Science sex difference (Cohen's d, girls vs boys)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Single regression weights on Cohen's d: GDP per capita β = 0.31; Gini Index β = 0.24; GET β = −0.11; GEP β = −0.07; GGI β = −0.06; GPI β = −0.08 (all not meaningful for GGI/GPI).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 1995-2019 Grade 8 science the study leveraged GDP per capita, Gini Index, and education spending indicators to predict the country-level sex difference in science (Cohen’s d), finding that boys’ relative advantage was smaller in more prosperous and more economically unequal nations (GDP β = 0.31; Gini β = 0.24) while public education investment showed small negative associations consistent with larger boys’ advantages (GET β = −0.11; GEP β = −0.07). This indicates that at later primary-to-lower-secondary transition ages, science sex gaps may depend more on the broader socioeconomic context than on gender-equality indices alone, implying that policy should consider national inequality and investment patterns together when designing interventions.

data.outcome_summary: This preregistered study uses PIRLS (2001–2016, grade 4 reading literacy) and TIMSS (1995–2019, grade 4 and grade 8 mathematics and science) to examine how country-level macro indicators predict cross-national sex differences in achievement. The dependent variables are country-level Cohen’s d sex differences computed from IEA-scaled plausible values; plausible-value-specific regressions are combined using Rubin (1987) rules. The paper reports standardized single-regression weights (β) rather than ML prediction metrics, and it does not train machine-learning models. Across domains, girls show consistent advantages in reading literacy, while mathematics and science sex differences are small on average but vary meaningfully by country and grade. The strongest and most consistent associations are observed for education investment and gender-related macro indicators in grade 4, with weaker or less systematic patterns for grade 8; limitations include correlational inference at the country level and incomplete reporting of missing-data handling for the macro predictor dataset.
